message.text: `StateTree.size` takes the whole tip's listing and goes straight on to `#sizes`, which runs `cat-file --batch-check` over every readable blob and builds a Map of all of them. It never checks `entryLimit` first. The memory this call uses for entries and sizes is therefore limited only by `listingLimit`, the 64 MiB of listing bytes, and not by the entry count that the git record store decision says bounds it.

evidence.snippet:
| Memory for the entries | 65,536 entries, `entryLimit`, checked before any size is read | `store.test.ts`, "the entries a tip may hold" |
| Memory for the listing of entries | 64 MiB, `listingLimit`, a KiB a line on average; git is stopped there, so the list never grows past it | `store.test.ts`, at the cap and one byte past it |
| A tip past either limit | No write of Melian's makes one: a write measures its commit by both limits before it pushes, and again after it rebuilds on a moved tip, and fails as `unreachable`, pushing nothing, when the commit would pass one. Dispose only shrinks the tip, so it works at either limit. A tip past a limit by another route still fails every call, dispose included. A writer on an older build or a push by hand can make one. A writer clears it by hand, removing files such as a changeset's folder in a commit of their own | `store.test.ts`, "the entries a write may leave" and "the bytes a tip may hold" |
| Memory for the sizes | One line per distinct readable blob, so the entry limit bounds it | the entry limit's tests |

- A call holds every entry of the tip too, so a tip of more than 65,536 entries, `entryLimit`, fails the call as `unreachable`, naming the branch, the count and the limit, before it reads a size. The listing is bounded first: git is stopped once it prints 64 MiB, `listingLimit`, a KiB a line on average, and the call fails the same way. A write measures the commit it built by both limits before it pushes, and again after it rebuilds on a tip that moved, so no write of Melian's takes the tip past one; a write that would fails as `unreachable` and pushes nothing. Dispose only shrinks the tip, so it works at either limit, and making room before a write is its job. Past a limit, every call but `retire` fails. `retire` reads only the top level of `changesets/` and the folders it was asked to remove, and pushes only a commit that `StateTree.removesOnly` finds removes whole changeset folders and nothing else, by `ls-tree`'s listing of the root and of `changesets/`, so it brings the tip back under; strays still need a writer with git. A retirement removes a folder only while its tree ID is the one its caller saw and its caller names it as merged, and never one that holds a stray or a cell, or whose name `changesets/` lists twice. Merged comes from GitHub's answer for that pull request, never from a record: a closed pull request can reopen at the same head and read a late relay's old round as standing. A cell holds a lease or a disposal mark, and rule 3 of the shared record decision never recreates such a changeset. It judges folders only while their entries and bytes together stay within the limits, and reports the rest as deferred, unread. `size()` counts what the limits measure, the tip's entries, its records' and cells' bytes and its listing's bytes, as a read counts them before it reads a blob, and answers on a tip past a limit too. Past the listing limit git is stopped, so it counts neither entries nor bytes and says so. `TipSize` imports nothing, so the `melian round` workflow's comment script reads a [cut at 2 KiB]

explanation.what: `StateTree.size` takes the whole tip's listing and goes straight on to `#sizes`, which runs `cat-file --batch-check` over every readable blob and builds a Map of all of them. It never checks `entryLimit` first. The memory this call uses for entries and sizes is therefore limited only by `listingLimit`, the 64 MiB of listing bytes, and not by the entry count that the git record store decision says bounds it.
explanation.whatToDo: Bound the work `size()` does by the entry limit. For example, when `listing.entries.length > entryLimit`, return the entry count and listing bytes but leave the record bytes uncounted, as `unlisted()` already does for the listing. Otherwise, add a row to the git record store decision's table recording that `size()` holds up to `listingLimit / ~55` entries and their sizes, and who accepted that.
explanation.whyHere: The base table under 'What one call uses, and what bounds it' says memory for the entries is bounded by '65,536 entries, `entryLimit`, checked before any size is read', and memory for the sizes by 'one line per distinct readable blob, so the entry limit bounds it'. `#measure` keeps that order: it checks the entry count at line 310 before `#sizes` at 315. The retirement decision also caps entries per folder before reading sizes. `size()` is built to answer on a tip past a limit, which is exactly the tip where the entry count can exceed 65,536. The change adds no row to the decision's table for this new resource, although the guideline it edits says a new resource must go there. The decision file was not edited.

properties.failureScenario: This needs a `melian/state` tip pushed past the entry limit by another route, which the decision table lists as reachable ('A writer on an older build or a push by hand can make one'). Take a tip of 1,000,000 small files with short paths. Each `ls-tree -r -z` line is about 55 to 64 bytes, so the listing stays under 64 MiB and `#list` does not truncate it. Running `melian doctor`, `melian records size`, or the round workflow's report step then calls `StateTree.size`. It builds 1,000,000 `TreeEntry` objects, each with its own copied `Buffer` path. It passes a stdin string of about 41 MB of object IDs to `cat-file --batch-check`, keeps the output (tens of MB) as one string, and builds a 1,000,000-entry Map. That is about 15 times the 65,536 entries the decision allows one call to hold. A normal read refuses this tip before reading a single size, but `size()` does the full work, using hundreds of MB of heap. In `doctor` it also risks running past the 20 s deadline. The documented bound on memory for entries and sizes therefore does not hold for this call.
